items.text: For a number in a table, use type.body. Don't use a mono font. Tables are rare and never compared column by column, so mono digits add nothing. The brand font keeps the voice.
For a supporting text, use type.caption. Don't use type.body. Fine print stays small, so the headlines keep the attention that wins sign-ups.
For a text in a table cell, use type.data. Don't use a mono font. It equals body here. Tables are rare and short. Cells keep the brand's text face, so they sound like the rest of the page.
For a parts of one item, use space.gap.tight. Don't use space.gap.default. An icon and its word sit close, so a call to action reads as one bold unit.

Inside a table cell, use space.inset.cell-x. Don't use narrow cell padding. Tables are rare, so cells keep the page's airy rhythm.

why: radius.pill: We use a pill corner for buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls in a playful tone, by brand convention. A full radius does this by rounding both ends into a capsule, the brand's signature shape. So every action feels bold and friendly, because the brand is bold (brand.q1), controls are pills (shape.values) and each section holds one big idea (content.q2).

radius.12: We use the 12px box corner for boxes that grow in order to keep them box-shaped objects by the relation: a pill control gives way to the box corner. A moderate radius does this by curving the corners while the sides stay straight as the box grows. So a text area or a list item stays a box, not an oval, because controls are pills (shape.values) and the brand is bold (brand.q1).

items.text: Inside a button or input, use space.inset.control-x. Don't use padding set by eye. Wide padding makes pill buttons bold and easy to hit with a thumb.
Inside a card, panel or dialog, use space.inset.container. Don't use text that touches the card edge. Generous padding lets each card hold its moment.
For an option in a menu or list, use radius.option. Don't use radius.control. Round options nest inside the round menu, so a menu feels as playful as the buttons.
For a something that grows past one line, use radius.element. Don't use radius.control. A pill corner breaks when a text area grows to many lines. The element corner stays round at any height.
For a corners of cards, menus and dialogs, use radius.surface. Don't use small corners. Big round corners make cards feel like friendly objects.
For a edges and dividers, use border-width.default. Don't use a hairline. A bold edge matches the bold type and vivid color.
For the curve of any move, use motion.easing.standard. Don't use a plain ease-out. An ease-out keeps every menu and button quick. The overshoot is kept for emphasis, where it feels alive and playful.
For an icon beside text, use size.icon and icon.stroke-width. Don't use a thin icon at text size. Larger icons hold their own next to big type. The thicker line carries the brand's warmth.

why: radius.pill: We use a pill corner for buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls in a playful tone, by brand convention. A full radius does this by rounding both ends into a capsule, the brand's signature shape. So every action feels bold and friendly, because the brand is bold (brand.q1), controls are pills (shape.values) and each section holds one big idea (content.q2).

radius.pill: We use the pill control corner for badges in order to keep one role family by the badge relation: badges share the control's corner. The same full radius does this by giving a status the capsule of the buttons beside it. So a status pill matches the buttons and the page keeps one shape, because badges get no corner of their own (shape.roles) and controls are pills (shape.values).

radius.20: We use a 20px corner for menu options in order to keep nesting by the relation: the 24px surface corner minus the panel's 4px padding. The inner radius does this by following the outer curve at the padding's distance. So an option's curve runs parallel to its menu's curve, because surfaces take 24px (shape.roles, brand.q1) and the panel's padding is 4px (spacing.values).

radius.12: We use the 12px box corner for boxes that grow in order to keep them box-shaped objects by the relation: a pill control gives way to the box corner. A moderate radius does this by curving the corners while the sides stay straight as the box grows. So a text area or a list item stays a box, not an oval, because controls are pills (shape.values) and the brand is bold (brand.q1).

radius.24: We use a 24px corner for cards, menus and dialogs in order to make each offer read as a separate object, in a bold tone by brand convention. A large radius does this by breaking the outline with a wide curve while the sides stay straight. So each offer reads as one friendly object, because containers get their own corner (shape.count) and the brand is bold (brand.q1).

brand-q3.answer: A display face for brand moments, with a sans for text
brand-q3.why: Bricolage Grotesque for display and headings, DM Sans for text: loud where the brand speaks, easy where people read.

items.label: Readability
items.text: Body text sits in DM Sans, a low-contrast sans that reads easily in short copy.

items.label: Legibility
items.text: DM Sans keeps simple, open shapes at small sizes; the display face never sets small text.

items.label: Scalability
items.text: Both are variable: Bricolage Grotesque has optical size, width and weight axes, and DM Sans optical size and weight.

items.label: Numerals
items.text: Numbers are few and set in DM Sans, in short copy rather than tables.

items.label: Scripts and languages
items.text: Latin, with accents; other scripts need faces chosen for the same voice.

items.label: Recognition
items.text: Bricolage Grotesque's character is the brand's: people know it by its headlines.

items.label: Familiarity
items.text: DM Sans for text keeps reading familiar while the display face takes the risks.

items.label: Personality
items.text: Bold and confident, as the brand answer asks.

items.label: Performance
items.text: Two variable families, one file each.

items.label: Licensing
items.text: SIL Open Font License, both: free to embed in apps and on the web.

items.label: Fallback and pairing
items.text: Falls back to system-ui, as its tokens say; DM Sans is the display face's text pair.

items.text: For a card on the page, use elevation.card (pronounced); none in dark. Don't use a flat card. Cards float to feel tactile. In dark a shade cannot be seen, so a lighter surface and a light ring lift them.

why: neutral.0, the same as content (surface.default): a menu stands out by its edge and its one shadow, not by its fill.
black.light.scrim: a see-through layer that dims the page behind a modal, so the dialog is the one thing to act on.

shadow.card: We use step 1 of the shadow scale for cards in order to show their height as objects above the page. The cast shade does this by a 12px offset and a 32px blur at 14%. So each offer feels like an object you can pick up, because cards rise too (elevation.roles) and shadows are pronounced (elevation.values).

shadow.overlay: We use step 2 of the shadow scale for menus and dialogs in order to show floating height, one step above the cards. The cast shade does this by a 24px offset and a 48px blur at 20%, larger than the card's. So a menu sits clearly above vivid sections and cards, because cards and overlays rise (elevation.roles) and shadows are pronounced (elevation.values).
neutral.100: We use one step lighter than content for menus, dialogs and raised cards in dark, in order to show height by tone,

on surface.default. The lighter fill does this by the dark-mode depth rule: the higher a layer sits, the lighter its surface. So visitors see a menu above the page even where its shadow barely shows, because dark ships as standard (theming.values) and the roles answer names the layers that rise (elevation.roles).
black.dark.scrim: a see-through layer that dims the page behind a modal, so the dialog is the one thing to act on.

shadow.none: We use no shadow for cards in dark in order to keep shadows on floating layers only: menus, popovers, dialogs, toasts and tooltips. The missing shade does this by leaving the card's height to tone: the lighter raised surface and its 1px light ring. So cards still read as lifted on a dark page, without a shade that cannot be seen, because dark ships as standard (theming.values) and cards rise by shadow in light (elevation.roles).

shadow.overlay-dark: We use the light overlay shadow's shape in dark in order to show the same floating height by the dark-shade relation. The cast shade does this by the same 24px offset and 48px blur, at 60% black instead of 20%. So a menu still sits above dark sections, though its shade reads weaker on dark than in light, because cards and overlays rise (elevation.roles) and dark ships as standard (theming.values).

items.text: For a paragraph or help text, use type.body, short. Don't use long paragraphs. Short copy keeps the energy.
For a button label, use a short verb that moves: Join, Try, Go. Don't use "Learn more". Big moments need verbs with energy.
For a success message, use celebrate, briefly. Don't use a long thank-you. A short celebration is remembered.
For an empty state, use playful, with a clear next step. Don't use a dead end. Playful words still need a way forward.
For a first visit, use one bold line and one button. Don't use a paragraph of copy. Visitors from a social post give a few seconds.
Toast's success tone. Celebrate, briefly: You're on the list. See you at launch.
